newsitem.title: USA: Study shows two-drug therapy helps HIV children.
newsitem.headline: Study shows two-drug therapy helps HIV children.

text.p: A study released on Thursday showed that, as with adults, children infected with HIV benefit more from a combination of drugs than from doses of a single drug.
The study, supported by the U.S. National Institutes of Health, involved 596 children aged between 42 days and 15 years at 87 different sites in the United States.

A combination of the AIDS cornerstone drug AZT with either of two other drugs "is far more effective at staving off disease progression or death in children with symptomatic HIV disease than using ddI (a single HIV-related drug) alone," the NIH said in a statement.
The study involved use of AZT (Glaxo-Wellcome's Retrovir) combined with 3TC (Glaxo-Wellcome's Epivir) or with ddI (Bristol-Myers Squibb's Videx) compared with use of ddI alone.

The statement said: "Combination antiretroviral therapy should be the preferred initial treatment for symptomatic HIV-infected children, particularly those under three years of age, who have never been treated with anti-HIV drugs."
It noted that in many cities in the northeastern United States "HIV disease is the leading cause of death among children aged two to five."

Anthony Fauci, director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, said the study, halted early because of the overwhelming result in favor of the combination of drugs, provided new hope for children with HIV.

"The preliminary results of this study clearly demonstrate that combination therapy can significantly slow disease progression and reduce the risk of death in HIV-infected children, as is the case in adults," he said.
Catherine Wilfert, scientific director of Pediatrics AIDS foundation, said the results were no surprise but substantiated earlier evidence.
She said one of the most encouraging signs was that children undergoing combination drug therapy grew in weight and height better than those on other treatment.

Ross McKinney of Duke University Medical Center in Durham, N.C., who chaired the study, said: "The findings increase the urgency to explore the effects in young children of more intensive combinations that include protease inhibitors."
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has said protease inhibitors, which are very expensive, may contribute to diabetes, although it does not recommend that patients stop taking them.
Last Thursday the U.S. Panel on Clinical Practices for Treatment of HIV Infection recommended three-drug therapy as the standard for adults.

And last Friday a team of international researchers said they had proved, in the largest trial of its kind, that a triple combination of drugs can help HIV-infected people live longer. That study involved adults.
